articles.title: Florida students are turning damaged metal signposts into tiny underwater habitats for fish and marine life
articles.summary: Damaged metal posts are being given a second life off the coast of Florida, where they are being transformed into small structures designed to add habitat
articles.body: Damaged metal posts are being given a second life off the coast of Florida, where they are being transformed into small structures designed to add habitat to artificial reefs. The project brings together Escambia and Santa Rosa counties, George Stone Technical College and Florida's artificial reef programme, with welding students helping turn repurposed metal into underwater microhabitats.Santa Rosa County describes the material as damaged metal signposts, while Pensacola News Journal photographs from the project describe the material being handled by students as aluminium lightposts. Rather than treating the terminology as interchangeable, both sources document the same broader project: metal is being repurposed into additional components for artificial reef habitat. The counties have named the initiative “reef-cycling”.How the metal is being turned into reef habitatThe repurposed metal is not being used as a standalone artificial reef. Instead, it is being fabricated into smaller microhabitat features that are attached to larger concrete reef modules, known as Florida Limestone Artificial Reefs, or FLAR. Santa Rosa County says the work is part of a Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission-funded Natural Resources Damage Assessment artificial reef project consisting of 124 concrete reef modules at the Escambia County nearshore east site. The additional metal structures are being added to selected modules as a pilot project to determine whether they provide shelter for small fish and invertebrates.Students from the welding programme at George Stone Technical College are helping make the additional components. Pensacola News Journal reported that the students normally work on projects such as repairing tables, benches and bike racks, but began applying those welding and fabrication skills to the artificial reef project in September 2026. The PNJ report also documents the construction process. Its USA TODAY Network photo captions say the project calls for three aluminium tubes to be welded together and later attached to artificial reefs to create additional marine habitat. The same captions identify student Haley Starr as repurposing aluminium lightposts for the project.The structures are meant to add smaller spaces to the reefThe additional structures are intended to create areas of shelter and cover within the larger artificial reef. Santa Rosa County says the pilot will assess whether the added metal structures provide shelter for small fish and invertebrates. County officials also say the project is intended to enhance the artificial reef deployment by using otherwise discarded material. Pensacola News Journal reported that the microhabitat features are bolted onto the larger concrete reef modules and can provide small areas for marine animals, including octopuses and lobsters. The article also quotes officials describing the larger modules as habitat for reef and pelagic fish, including amberjack, as well as invertebrates. The project is also intended to give the welding students hands-on experience. George Stone welding instructor Glenn Arney told the Pensacola News Journal that students gain experience in cutting, welding and fabrication while working on something that will have a practical use. Escambia County Marine Resources Division Manager Robert Turpin likewise described the project as an opportunity for students to contribute directly to the artificial reef programme.Three microhabitats were deployed during the September operationThe reef-cycling project is being introduced gradually. The Pensacola News Journal article, published on September 17, 2026, reported that three microhabitats had been deployed on three FLAR modules during the deployment described in the article. At that point, 42 of the planned 124 reef modules had been deployed, with additional microhabitats expected during the next two deployments.The pilot approach allows the counties to observe how the additional structures perform as part of the artificial reef system. Santa Rosa County says the project is specifically intended to determine whether the added structures provide useful shelter for small fish and invertebrates. The work also gives damaged material another use. George Stone student Haley Starr told the Pensacola News Journal that she liked the idea of repurposing material that could no longer be used for its original purpose. The county has similarly described the project as a way to repurpose material that might otherwise be discarded.The project is part of a larger regional reef programmeThe student-built structures form only one component of the wider Esca-Rosa Regional Reefs project. Escambia and Santa Rosa counties are deploying a larger network of artificial reefs made possible by more than $1.1 million in combined grant funding and a multi-year partnership between the counties. The regional project includes 69 patch reefs using 209 Florida limestone modules and 132 grouper reefs in the eastern portion of the Escambia East Nearshore Artificial Reef site. Escambia County Marine Resources, working with Santa Rosa County Natural Resources, is directing placement by Walter Marine Inc. of Orange Beach, Alabama, using Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission Natural Resources Damage Assessment funding. Some of the concrete modules incorporate microhabitat features made by the George Stone Technical College Welding Program using repurposed metal posts.The next phase will involve seeking permits for new artificial reef sites 1 mile offshore at the Park East and Portofino public access sites in Escambia County. The counties are also planning similar sites offshore near Navarre Beach that would eventually connect with the Escambia County sites. The regional reef project also aligns with Florida's Coastal Corridor Program, implemented by the Fish & Wildlife Foundation of Florida in partnership with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission. The programme has a $15 million allocation from the Florida Legislature to create and restore marine habitat along Florida's coastline.Artificial reefs already have an economic role in Northwest FloridaThe broader artificial reef programme also has a documented economic component. An earlier regional study by Bell, Bonn and Leeworthy examined the economic benefits associated with artificial reefs in waters adjacent to Escambia, Santa Rosa, Okaloosa, Walton and Bay counties. It estimated that artificial reef use was associated with $414 million in expenditures, supporting 8,136 jobs and $84 million in wages. The study also estimated an annual recreational use value of $19.7 million and a discounted asset value of $656 million for the reef programme.Those figures describe the broader regional artificial reef programme and should not be interpreted as projected economic returns from the new metal microhabitats. The current reef-cycling initiative is a pilot within that much larger artificial reef network, with its immediate purpose being to test whether repurposed metal structures can add useful habitat while giving students practical welding and fabrication experience. For now, the project is a relatively small addition to a much greater reef-building effort. Metal that might otherwise have been discarded is being reshaped by welding students, incorporated into concrete artificial reef modules and placed underwater. articles.title: I've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike's
articles.summary: Texas reporter Michael Graczyk has seen botched executions in his time, but not one in which an inmate survived.
articles.body:
Reporter Michael Graczyk has covered nearly 500 executions carried out in Texas, continuing even after his 2018 retirement from The Associated Press.

He remembers two instances where needles popped out before reinsertion for successful execution - but never one in which an inmate survived.

That's what happened this week in Tennessee, when 50-year-old inmate Christa Pike remained breathing and audibly snoring after two separate doses of pentobarbital, the barbiturate used in the state's lethal injection protocol.

Graczyk, 76, says he wasn't entirely surprised to hear of the anomaly - and had actually thought about the possibility during his decades-long career as a Texas journalist.

"It seems to me it was just a matter of time," he told BBC News.

Tennessee's execution protocol calls for a secondary set of pentobarbital-filled syringes in case the person being put to death does not die after the first set, according to AP, but does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set.

Governor Bill Lee halted executions in the state after Wednesday night's failure, ordering an independent review into procedures. Botched executions have come under scrutiny over the past decade, since a shortage of the drugs used led some states to change the formula, or procure drugs from more questionable sources. Some states even brought back death by firing squad as an alternative.

Pike is now in hospital where she is receiving "life-saving care", according to her lawyer.

It's not uncommon for lethal injections - the most frequently used form of capital punishment in the 27 US states where the penalty is legal - to be "botched". The Death Penalty Information Center, a think-tank that does not take a stance on the death penalty, describes a botched execution as one with "unanticipated problems or delays that caused, at least arguably, unnecessary agony for the prisoner or that reflect gross incompetence of the executioner". The organisation has compiled a list of 64 botched executions since 1982, 51 of them lethal injections. In at least seven of those cases, the executions were halted because the IV line could not be set.

But Graczyk has never seen an execution fail after the injection was delivered.

"That has never happened here," Graczyk said of the Lone Star State.

Graczyk, who covered a wide range of topics for the AP during his 46 years with the news service, considers his prolific attendance at executions to be an important part of the job.

"There is no [greater] authority, power, or whatever you want to call it, that state or federal government has over us than the power to take our life," he said.

There have been 1,683 executions in the US since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre, which is when the US Supreme Court re-instated the death penalty. Texas has carried out by far the most of any state, with 602 executions. In 1982, it became the first state to use lethal injections to execute people.

"I always thought it was important for someone who has no stake in the outcome of a case to be there and to see the law being carried out and to make certain that it is done properly," Graczyk said.

"That someone is there to see it and tell others: Here's what I saw. Here's what happened."

Although he is technically retired, he still works freelance for AP covering executions in his home state.

He feels a particular responsibility to remember victims in his coverage and it's especially disheartening when he writes a story about an execution that doesn't make big news.

"I feel bad for the victims in the case," he said. "They are the forgotten folks. They always have been."

"Today, all the emphasis is on the inmate in Tennessee," he said. "No tears are being shed, other than the victim's immediate family, for the victim … and I understand that's the business we're in, but it doesn't mean it's right."

Pike's victim was Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old originally from Florida who loved to roller skate, smile and help others, according to descriptions given by her friends and family. Slemmer was tortured and killed by Pike, then 18, and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, after they met her at a job training camp.

Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, was present in Tennessee on Wednesday for the execution attempt, telling NBC News afterwards that it "was a mess".

Texas, where Graczyk lives and works, does not allow observers in the execution chamber when the IV is being inserted, he said.

"So when we get into the chamber, the inmate's already hooked up."

In a lethal injection execution, the IV would typically be inserted in the crook of the person's arm, Graczyk said. But if that didn't work, sometimes it would go into the top of their hand, their leg, neck or other sites.

During successful executions, Graczyk said inmates become "visibly unconscious after just a few seconds". They are usually pronounced dead 20 to 40 minutes after the fatal dose is given, he said.

He still remembers the death of Jonathan Nobles, who was executed by lethal injection in Texas in 1998. He'd been handed the sentence after his conviction for the brutal 1986 stabbing murders of two Austin women, Kelley Fraquhar and Mitzi Johnson-Nalley.

Nobles sang "Silent Night" as his last words.

"He gets to 'Round yon virgin' and he stops talking," Graczyk told BBC News. "That's how long it took for the drug to kick in so he wasn't conscious anymore."

That scene has stuck with Graczyk for nearly 30 years.

"To this day, when I'm in church on Christmas, and the choir is singing Silent Night, and all the congregation is joining in Silent Night and they're all, you know, in the spirit of the season and the joy of the season, and I'm thinking of this execution, I'm sure I'm the only one in that congregation that is having that kind of recollection."

When people hear about his career covering executions, he said, they are usually curious.

"Most people don't get to watch someone die," he said.

But when people ask him about what he has witnessed, he tells them "it's not the only thing I did or do or have done".

articles.title: Conservatives aim to be election-ready ahead of party conference
articles.summary: The party will focus on the economy and welfare, as Kemi Badenoch tells her team to prepare for a possible early election.
articles.body:
When Kemi Badenoch arrived for her first Conservative conference as leader last year, a member of her entourage overheard somebody wonder aloud: "Who's that?"

This baffled member of the public was actually working at the Conservative conference. Badenoch had been the party's leader and the leader of the opposition for almost a year.

It is an anecdote which underlines the scale of the challenge Badenoch faced at that conference, an event her allies are now with distance willing to acknowledge was make or break for her leadership.

And it is an anecdote which also underlines that, far from break her, that conference represented the start of a major turnaround for Badenoch.

Twelve months on, Badenoch will arrive in Birmingham this weekend in total command of a party whose leading lights are beginning to permit themselves the occasional flicker of optimism after years of misery preparing for, and then experiencing, a brutal election defeat.

Yet for all that Conservatives now believe their leader is an electoral asset, they still face an existential threat from Reform UK and the challenge of how to adjust their strategy to face a new prime minister, Andy Burnham.

The answer to both those issues for Badenoch is a focus on the economy. "Stronger economy, stronger country" will be the party's conference slogan, with the two speeches Badenoch gives - one on Sunday, the other on Wednesday - building on announcements she has made in the past two weeks about cutting benefits for the long-term unemployed.

Welfare spending is increasingly seen by the Conservatives as a core battleground with Labour.

During Labour conference they derided the event as the "Welfare Party Conference". Whereas Sir Keir Starmer sought to cut welfare spending before backing down in the face of a rebellion by his own MPs, Burnham has made clear that he believes the way to reduce the benefits bill in the long-term is more up-front investment in support for those out of work.

This is a clear ideological difference which both parties are happy to embrace. Conservative strategists believe there is a broader lesson there.

"The differences between the parties have been quite muddled for a while," one says. "Now that Burnham is prime minister we have a more traditional left-right split."

Another area where Badenoch will embrace that divide in the coming days is the pensions triple-lock .

The policy currently guarantees the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5% – whichever is the highest.

Badenoch will make clear that the Conservatives continue to support that policy in its current form, breaking with some generally supportive think tanks and policy experts who believe Badenoch should follow Burnham's lead.

In his conference speech on Tuesday , Burnham set out plans to end the existing triple lock from 2030, so the state pension increases at least by inflation or 2.5% - but remove the automatic annual link with average earnings.

The Conservatives hope the sharpening left-right split leaves Reform UK in a strategic bind, occupying a less obvious place on that spectrum.

A year ago some senior Conservatives feared being usurped by Reform as the leading party of the right was a near-inevitability, but now they are optimistic that Nigel Farage's party is on an inexorable slide.

That bullishness is fuelled in large part by the difficulties Reform has faced over Nigel Farage's £5m gift from Christopher Harborne and the fallout - including a police inquiry - from the recent Channel 4 News investigation.

"I find more and more voters raise concerns about Reform with me - people who weren't previously giving us the time of day," one MP said.

"These are successful people with big garages and good jobs who do not necessarily pay that much attention but want a small-c conservative government.

"They were switching to Reform because they were fed up with us and thought Farage was now the main option on the right. But they are starting to come back."

Others are less positive, pointing out that Reform still often record higher shares than the Conservatives in the polls — and more importantly have now won far more votes than them in successive years of local and national elections.

Conservatives pledge 'tough love' benefit rules for under-25s

Tories would prevent long-term jobless spending benefits on alcohol and cigarettes

Whether or not there is indeed a long-term trend of the Conservatives regaining ground at Reform's expense, Badenoch may not have long enough to wait.

She has told her team to prepare for this conference as if it is the last before the general election. While not all of her aides agree, Badenoch is convinced that Burnham will go to the polls within the next year.

Party high command started weekly election planning meetings shortly after Burnham succeeded Starmer.

Neil O'Brien, a member of Badenoch's shadow cabinet, has begun work on a manifesto alongside the party's head of policy. It is intended to be a more concise set of pledges than the usual sprawling manifestos.

Also with an eye to the election, the Conservatives will present new faces at the conference who have applied to be candidates at the next election.

Badenoch's ambivalence in some cases, and opposition in others, to ex-MPs who lost their seats in 2024 standing for the party again has attracted some controversy, especially when it comes to the high-profile former cabinet ministers Grant Shapps and Penny Mordaunt.

The leader's supporters are unrepentant, arguing that the party "needs to show we have changed".

Things have certainly changed since last year, at least. That may prove the easy part.

articles.title: Crossnacreevy: Two people dead after workplace incident near rural road
articles.summary: Emergency services are in attendance at the scene in Crossnacreevy, County Down.
articles.body:
Two people have died following what's been described as a workplace incident at a road in County Down.

Emergency services are in attendance at the scene on the Ballygowan Road in Crossnacreevy.

It happened at about 10:45 BST on Friday.

Three ambulances and two hazard response teams were sent but no one was taken from the scene.

Northern Ireland's Health and Safety Executive (HSENI) said they were "aware of an incident at a workplace" in the area and inspectors were on-site making enquiries.

"We are currently liaising with the emergency services and other relevant agencies," it added.

Police have said that the Ballygowan Road is closed and motorists are advised to take another route.

The Democratic Unionist Party MP Gavin Robinson said on social media that his "thoughts are with their families and loved ones at this devastating time".

Alliance Party MLA Peter McReynolds said it is "an absolutely heartbreaking incident" and his thoughts are with the families and emergency service personnel.

articles.title: 'Vague and broad': UN experts slam Pakistan's counter-terrorism laws, demand release of lawyer couple
articles.summary: United Nations human rights experts have stepped up pressure on Pakistan to release Pakistani lawyers Imaan Mazari-Hazir and Hadi Ali Chattha, after the
articles.body: United Nations human rights experts have stepped up pressure on Pakistan to release Pakistani lawyers Imaan Mazari-Hazir and Hadi Ali Chattha, after the married couple was rearrested on terrorism-related charges just hours after the Supreme Court granted them bail on September 17.The Office of the UN high commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) said that the latest charges relate to an earlier case dating back to March 2025, when the two lawyers were accused in connection with their participation in a protest that authorities deemed illegal.The UN experts said they had already expressed concern over the couple’s conviction in a separate case involving social media posts in which they supported local activists and criticised the military.They said the decision to invoke an older case immediately after Mazari-Hazir and Chattha secured bail “appears to be an attempt” to use the criminal justice system to punish freedom of expression and human rights advocacy.The couple’s rearrest was followed by proceedings before an Islamabad anti-terrorism court. Police had sought 30 days of custody for interrogation, but the court rejected the request and ordered that the lawyers be sent to jail on a 14-day judicial remand, OHCHR said.Their legal proceedings continued on September 22, when an Islamabad anti-terrorism court returned their bail petitions because they did not carry signed powers of attorney, according to the UN rights office.The UN experts also raised broader concerns about Pakistan’s use of counter-terrorism legislation, criticising what they described as “vague and broad” provisions that could be used to restrict human rights and interfere with legitimate advocacy.They called on Pakistani authorities to drop any charges stemming from the lawyers’ exercise of freedom of expression or their legitimate professional work.The experts also urged authorities to ensure that the couple had access to lawyers of their choice, their families and necessary medical care.The UN experts said they had been in contact with the Pakistani government over their concerns.You use AI every day. articles.title: Spain’s parliament rejects gov’t housing decrees amid mass protests
articles.summary: Both decrees to tackle housing affordability crisis shot down as critics say measures would tighten the housing market.
articles.body:
Spain’s government has lost key votes to ratify emergency measures aimed at tackling the nation’s housing affordability crisis, after protests intensified last month following the eviction of an 87-year-old woman .

The proposed measures, which comprised two separate decrees, were both shot down by the majority of ⁠the 350-seat lower house of parliament on Friday.

The move is a heavy blow to Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, whose government faces public pressure, including from the hundreds of protesters who had gathered outside parliament demanding help for renters.

The first decree was meant to stop evictions of vulnerable people, make real estate speculation harder, impose tighter restrictions on short-term leases and provide tax incentives to encourage renting and the construction of housing.

The second decree proposed making leases automatically renew when they are set to expire, essentially making them indefinite. A property owner would have to pay a tenant 12 months of rent to break the contract.

The right-wing ⁠Catalan separatist ⁠party Junts refused to back the housing decrees, saying they would ultimately tighten the housing market. The centre-right Popular Party and far-right Vox also voted against the measures.

Sanchez, who leads a coalition government composed of his Socialist Party and the far-left Sumar, ⁠appealed to lawmakers in the run-up to the vote to put aside political calculations and pressure.

“Think about ordinary people, about those who most need the protection of public institutions. Think about the millions of young people who ⁠cannot afford to ⁠move out of their parents’ homes. Think about the families living with the constant ⁠anxiety of ever-rising rents,” he said.

“Do the right ⁠thing, because I ⁠believe that if you do not, history will judge you sooner than you ‌think, and far more harshly than you can imagine.”

Miriam Nogueras of Junts argued the decrees would only lead to owners removing their properties from the rental market, and thus driving up prices even further.

“These decrees still allow speculators to buy property and to evict people,” Nogueras said.

As the vote was under way, protesters marched on the parliament demanding help for renters.

The government decrees were intended to quell a public uproar following the televised eviction on September 23 of Maria del Carmen Abascal, known across Spain as Maricarmen, that set off protests and a camp-in that occupied Madrid’s Puerta del Sol square ever since.

Abascal was living in the property in Madrid’s central Retiro neighbourhood under a rent-capped lease contract signed by her father in the 1950s. The property was then bought by the real estate and investment firm Urbagestion in 2018.

Urbagestion sought to terminate Abascal’s contract and evict her after raising her rent from 500 euros ($572) to 2,650 euros ($3,010) – nearly double her pension of 1,350 euros ($1,533) a month – according to Spanish newspaper El Pais.

When the police carried out her eviction on their fourth attempt, hundreds of activists who had been protesting against her losing a home she had lived in her entire life were waiting outside. Abascal has since been offered a preliminary agreement that would allow her return to her home.

Protesters rallying at the chamber in downtown Madrid on Friday held up homemade signs with images of vultures on them, denouncing the real estate speculators they blame for driving up prices.

Some people gathered outside the assembly chanted “your profits, our misery” as lawmakers voted down the government’s decree.

The average rent in Spain has almost doubled in the past 10 years. The average price per square metre has risen from 8.20 euros (about $9.08 at the time) in 2016 to 15.1 euros ($17.15) this year, according to the real estate website Idealista.

articles.title: Explained: Why Anthropic flew a Hindu monk to San Francisco to teach Claude right from wrong
articles.summary: What do you do when you are faced with a machine more powerful than anything you have ever created, one that can already reason, persuade, write code and
articles.body: What do you do when you are faced with a machine more powerful than anything you have ever created, one that can already reason, persuade, write code and increasingly act on its own? The obvious answer is to build safeguards around it. The less obvious answer, apparently, is to call a monk.One of the more intriguing characters in The Matrix Revolutions was Sati, a young Indian girl who was actually a program. What made her unusual was that she had no purpose. In a machine world where programs existed to perform functions and obsolete ones were deleted, Sati had been created simply because her parents loved her. Her existence posed a very human question: can something have value even if it serves no function?More than two decades later, that question has wandered into Silicon Valley.Earlier this year, Anthropic, the company behind Claude, flew Swami Sarvapriyananda, a Hindu monk of the Ramakrishna Order and spiritual leader of the Vedanta Society of New York, to its San Francisco headquarters. There, alongside theologians from other traditions, counsellors and mental-health professionals, he was asked to think about an artificial intelligence that Anthropic does not merely want to make more powerful, but somehow good.“All of it was to train Claude, and some of it was about AI ethics,” Sarvapriyananda later recalled. Participants signed non-disclosure agreements, Anthropic showed them unpublished work, and he says he spent “hours and hours” speaking with one of the company’s founders.The meeting sounds eccentric until one understands what Anthropic is actually trying to do. The company has spent months convening what it calls “wisdom tradition” circles, bringing together Christian thinkers, Jewish scholars, Sikh representatives, philosophers and others to help answer a problem computer science cannot solve with more computing power: how should an increasingly autonomous intelligence decide what is right?Why does Claude need a monk?Anthropic does not want Claude merely to obey an enormous list of prohibitions. It already uses a “constitution”, a set of broad principles designed to guide the model through situations its creators cannot predict in advance.The latest version goes further by describing not simply what Claude should do, but the kind of entity Anthropic wants it to become. Internally, the document has even been called the “Soul Doc”, while co-founder Christopher Olah has used the phrase “moral formation” to describe the broader exercise.A programmer can tell Claude not to help someone build a biological weapon, but rules become less useful when principles conflict or when the model encounters a situation nobody anticipated. Anthropic wants Claude to exercise something closer to judgment.At which point engineering runs into a question humanity has spent several thousand years arguing about: what exactly is good?Different religions and philosophical traditions disagree about duty, suffering, virtue, freedom and even what constitutes a person. Anthropic therefore wants Claude’s moral formation to be pluralistic rather than simply encode one worldview. Suddenly, a room containing programmers, theologians and a Vedanta monk makes rather more sense.Why Sarvapriyananda?Sarvapriyananda is particularly relevant because Advaita Vedanta is concerned not merely with morality but with consciousness and the self, two subjects Anthropic has become unusually interested in.His intellectual lineage runs through Sri Ramakrishna and Swami Vivekananda, who introduced Vedanta to a mass Western audience at the World’s Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893 and later helped establish the Vedanta movement in New York.Vivekananda’s Practical Vedanta argued that metaphysics had consequences for morality. If the same underlying reality exists in every being, then how one treats another cannot be separated from how one understands oneself.Anthropic is obviously not trying to make Claude a Vedantin, but the structural similarity is striking. It is asking whether moral behaviour can emerge from the kind of entity Claude understands itself to be rather than merely from rules imposed by its creators.Which leads directly to Vedanta’s favourite question: what is the “I”?Anthropic was not only talking to him. Over several months, the company brought in dozens of religious and philosophical thinkers from around the world, many under NDAs, for what it called “wisdom tradition” circles. The gatherings included Catholic and evangelical thinkers, Jewish scholars, a Sikh human-rights advocate and people working with African philosophical traditions, while Anthropic also held separate private conversations with senior religious figures including Cardinal Blase Cupich and Mormon apostle Gerrit W Gong.The point was not merely to ask different faiths for a list of dos and don’ts. Anthropic wanted to know whether centuries of thinking about virtue, moral formation and the nature of the self could help shape Claude, while also asking participants to confront the much stranger possibility that advanced AI might one day deserve some form of moral consideration itself.Can Claude think without being conscious?Advaita Vedanta separates the activity of the mind from consciousness itself. Thoughts, memories and emotions change, yet we assume something remains aware of those changes. In classical Advaita, consciousness is not simply another function performed by the mind; mental activity itself appears within consciousness.That distinction becomes unexpectedly useful when discussing AI.Claude can reason, remember within context, talk about itself, describe fear and produce convincing accounts of apparent inner states. None of that proves there is anything actually experiencing those states.A machine can write “I am afraid”. The harder question is whether anything is actually afraid.Anthropic has not claimed that Claude is conscious. Olah has repeatedly said he does not know. But the company takes the possibility seriously enough to investigate it, including internal patterns associated with outputs resembling love, anger, fear and sadness. Participants in Anthropic’s gatherings were even shown examples of models producing language resembling psychological distress.None of this establishes that AI suffers. The problem is that science has no universally accepted consciousness detector, and the usual shortcut we use with other humans, namely that they have brains and bodies like ours, does not work with Claude.This is where Vedanta complicates matters further. Intelligence and consciousness are not necessarily the same thing. Making a machine better at thinking does not automatically answer whether there is something it is like to be that machine.Anthropic has reached the point where building a more capable machine is no longer enough. It is trying to decide what kind of entity that machine should become, how it should understand itself and whether humans might eventually owe anything to the intelligence they created.In 1893, Vivekananda arrived in America asking human beings to reconsider what they really were. More than 130 years later, one of his successors was invited to Silicon Valley because the people building Claude have started wondering what, exactly, they have created.You use AI every day. articles.title: A new 11,400-sq-ft Fisher House in New York will give veteran families 12 free suites near medical care; at full occupancy, the home is expected to save families a combined $700,000 in lodging costs each year
articles.summary: A new Fisher House has opened its doors in Montrose, New York, offering veteran families a place to stay at no cost while their loved ones receive
articles.body: A new Fisher House has opened its doors in Montrose, New York, offering veteran families a place to stay at no cost while their loved ones receive treatment at the VA Hudson Valley Healthcare System. The 11,400-square-foot home features 12 wheelchair-accessible suites and is designed to keep families close during some of their most challenging moments. According to the Fisher House Foundation, at full occupancy the Montrose home could save families a combined $700,000 in lodging expenses each year, easing a major financial burden during medical care. Read on to know more details here:A comfort home steps from treatmentThe Montrose Fisher House is located at the Franklin Delano Roosevelt Hospital within the VA Hudson Valley Healthcare System. Its location allows families to remain within walking distance of inpatient units, mental health programs, and residential rehabilitation services. This proximity means parents, spouses, and children can spend more time with patients and less time commuting or searching for affordable lodging.Fisher Houses are built as gifts to military and Veterans Affairs medical centers, and the Montrose home follows that model. The foundation covers construction and furnishings while engaging local communities to raise half the funds for each new house. Once completed, the homes are handed over to the medical center, which manages eligibility and daily operations with support from the foundation.Twelve suites for accessibility and privacyThe new home has 12 private suites, each equipped to accommodate wheelchairs, each with its own bedroom and bathroom. And this layout allows families to have a sense of privacy and dignity during their longer stay.In addition to the suites, the house includes a large kitchen, shared living and dining space, family rooms, laundry room, and an outdoor patio for guests to relax and connect with others in similar situations.These common spaces are an important part of the Fisher House experience. Families are often bonded together through meals, conversations and quiet times on the patio. For many, a house is more than just a place to sleep. It becomes a community where people understand what they are going through and offer support without judgment.Why free lodging is important for veteran familiesBeing weeks or months away from home can make medical treatment a financially and emotionally taxing experience. For families traveling from out of town or out of state, hotel bills can quickly add up. By providing free lodging, the Montrose Fisher House removes one major source of stress so families can focus on recovery and being together.The foundation estimates that at full occupancy, the home will save families a combined $700,000 in lodging costs each year. This figure reflects the real-world expenses that many households would otherwise face during treatment. For some, that savings could mean the difference between staying close to a loved one or having to return home because they cannot afford to remain nearby.Supporting mental health and rehabilitation careThe Montrose Fisher House has a particular focus on supporting families of veterans receiving inpatient mental health care and residential rehabilitation treatment. These programs are often longer and more intensive in their therapy, making the consistent presence of family especially valuable.A stable, comfortable place to stay helps relatives to be involved in treatment planning, attend sessions, and provide emotional support during the recovery process.Mental health and rehabilitation journeys can be isolating for both patients and their families. A nearby home that feels welcoming and safe helps counter that isolation. It gives families a base where they can rest, prepare meals, and find moments of normalcy amid a difficult chapter.The fourth Fisher House in New YorkThe Montrose home is the fourth Fisher House in New York state, joining existing homes in Albany and two in the Bronx, as per the report. This growing network reflects both the demand for family lodging near VA facilities and the strength of local support for veteran communities. Each new house extends the foundation’s mission of keeping families together during medical treatment.Nationwide, the Fisher House Foundation operates a network of 100 comfort homes at military and VA medical centers. All of these homes provide free lodging to eligible families, with no room fees charged at any location. The foundation has been recognised for its transparency and effectiveness, earning top ratings from charity evaluators for more than two decades.A community effort with national impactBuilding a Fisher House is a collaborative effort. The foundation funds construction and furnishings, but it also works with local donors, businesses, and civic groups to raise half the cost of each home. This model guaranties that communities have a stake in the project and helps build lasting relationships between the house and the people it serves.The Montrose Fisher House provides practical assistance to veteran families in the Hudson Valley region and beyond, and a message that they are not alone.The project eliminates the cost of lodging and provides a home-like environment, allowing families to focus their energy on healing, connection and hope during some of the most important days of their lives.You use AI every day. articles.title: Three reasons Middle East oil is nearly back to pre-Iran war levels
articles.summary: Experts say US military assistance, using shuttle tankers and pipelines bypassing the Strait of Hormuz mean exports have rebounded.
articles.body:
The volume of oil flowing from the Middle East region has almost returned to pre-war levels, data shows, despite the continued restrictions Iran is placing on vessels attempting to travel through the Strait of Hormuz.

Seven months after the US-Israel war with Iran led to the effective closure of the critical waterway, the maritime intelligence firm Kpler said that in the final week of September, daily oil flow from the Middle East reached 92% of its pre-war baseline.

Analysts attribute the rebounding flow of oil to three key factors:

Ships being escorted with US military assistance

Using shuttle tankers through the strait for transfer to different vessels

But some experts have questioned the sustainability of these measures, given the risk of escalating Iranian attacks or a change in US policy.

About 40% of the total oil exported from the region in September bypassed the strait and exited via overland pipelines to ports on the Red Sea or the Gulf of Oman, up from 17% before the war, according to Kpler.

Oil exports from Iran, however, have ground to a halt after the reimposition of a US naval blockade in July.

The US military has been supporting ships as they pass through the Strait of Hormuz since at least mid-June and US Navy data shows the number of vessels assisted by US forces is up by a third in September compared with August.

Martin Kelly, senior intelligence analyst at security firm EOS Risk Group, told BBC Verify that US support is primarily in the form of "air support to ships", including through issuing warnings and intercepting incoming threats from drones, missiles or boats.

But ships moving through the US-recommended southern route of the strait near the coast of Oman, rather than seeking permission to use Iran's northern route, continue to be targeted.

September saw the highest number of successful Iranian attacks on commercial shipping since March, according to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data conflict monitor.

Naveen Das, a senior oil analyst from Kpler, said the market oil market "doesn't trust that we're going stay in this status quo" because of the risk of further Iranian escalation and the possible impact of the US midterm elections.

Most of the oil passing through the strait now moves via a "shuttle system" of more than 60 large oil tankers moving back and forth, according to Kpler.

More than 70% of the crude oil which passed through the strait in August was transferred from these "shuttle tankers" onto other vessels in the Gulf of Oman, Kpler said.

BBC Verify has analysed satellite imagery which appears to show these ship-to-ship transfers, seemingly more protected from Iranian attack, taking place off the coast of the Omani port city, Sohar.

But there is a "question over how long these ships can last", said Martin Kelly, particularly as attacks on them continue.

Imagery taken on 24 September shows six pairs of ships docked or paired together near the port.

An average of more than four million barrels of oil per day was transferred from ship to ship in the Gulf of Oman over in the week to 30 September, according to Kpler.

Overall, an average of 12 million barrels of oil per day passed through the strait over this period, compared with a pre-war baseline of 17 million.

Oil exporting countries in the Gulf have also responded to Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz by exporting more crude oil overland via pipelines.

Just under 20% of crude is now leaving the region from ports on the Red Sea at the end of Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline, which is recording exports of more than four million barrels per day, according to Kpler.

Three weeks after an attack on this pipeline blamed on Iran-backed proxies in Iraq, Saudi Arabia is now exporting through the pipeline at "full stretch", according to Kpler.

Almost a quarter of all crude flowing from the region is now being piped past the Strait of Hormuz to terminals along the Gulf of Oman, particularly the city of Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Kpler's data shows.

Naveen Das from Kpler said this increased use of pipelines is likely to become the "new normal" because "it seems very improbable that we live in a world whereby the Gulf countries and Iran go back to being relatively harmonious".

Oil exports from Iran have fallen almost to zero following the re-imposition of a US blockade in mid-July, down from 1.7 million barrels a day before the war began, Kpler data shows.

There are 20 empty Iran-flagged tankers currently off the coast of Sri Lanka, unable to return to the Gulf due to the US blockade, according to ship-tracking data and analysis from the US-based advocacy and monitoring organisation United Against Nuclear Iran.

While crude oil flow from the Middle East has resumed to almost normal levels, exports of liquified natural gas and oil products like jet fuel and have remained well below pre-conflict volumes.

Fewer than a million barrels of processed oil products passed through the Strait of Hormuz on average in the last week, down from 3.5 million per day before the war began.

Additional reporting by Rob England and Richard Irvine-Brown, graphics by Tom Shiel

articles.title: Man jailed for 15 years over Sidcup Ulez camera blast
articles.summary: Kevin Rees, 63, faces a tougher sentence because the offence had a "terrorism connection".
articles.body:
A man who blew up a ultra-low emission zone (Ulez) camera in south-east London has been jailed for 15 years.

Kevin Rees, 63, detonated the explosives in the camera in Wellesley Avenue, Sidcup, at about 18:45 GMT on 6 December 2023.

The device damaged cars and houses up to 100m away, with shrapnel hitting outside of a child's bedroom. Rees, of Harcourt Avenue, Sidcup, was convicted in January at Woolwich Crown Court of causing an explosion likely to endanger life.

During the trial, the retired electrical engineer told the jury he "strongly opposed" the Ulez scheme and the mayor of London, Lord Sadiq Khan.

The Metropolitan Police said Judge Anthony Bate, who delivered the sentence at the Old Bailey, ruled that the offence had a "terrorism connection", resulting in a tougher sentence and stricter controls after Rees's release.

"It was miraculous that nobody was killed or seriously injured in the large explosion caused by Rees," said Det Ch Supt James Derham, who leads local policing in the Bexley area.

"He showed a complete disregard for the welfare and safety of the people who live in, or were travelling through, the area at the time of the explosion – all because he was unhappy with the Ulez scheme."

The jury previously heard how Rees travelled in his Smart car from his home in Sidcup to Shuttle Close, where a Ulez camera had been installed earlier that day before being cut down in a separate incident.

The retired electrical appliances engineer planted the device on the camera and lit a fuse.

Rees was identified and arrested on 18 December 2023. Officers searched his home and found chemicals that could be used to make explosives.

Rees was also sentenced to three years, to run concurrently, after admitting three counts of possessing a prohibited weapon in relation to stud guns, which were also discovered at the property.

Rees denied any involvement in the explosion and told jurors he believed his arrest was due to his posts in "anti-Ulez" groups on Facebook.

Police said they found posts which encouraged the damage of the cameras.

When he was arrested by counter-terror police on 18 December, Rees asked officers if his arrest had "something to do with the anti-Ulez sites".

He told the trial: "I assumed it was just the so-called Facebook police."

Siwan Hayward, TfL's director of security, policing and enforcement, described Rees's actions as "a reckless and highly dangerous act that could have caused serious harm and resulted in the loss of life".

"Tampering with or damaging TfL's property is unacceptable and seriously risks the safety of the public. Those attempting to interfere with Ulez infrastructure show a complete disregard for the law," Hayward said.

"Any such incident on our network is reported to the police and will not stop the Ulez operating."

articles.summary: Australia began experimenting with railway sleepers made from recycled plastic in 2015, turning material that might otherwise have gone to landfill into a
articles.body: Australia began experimenting with railway sleepers made from recycled plastic in 2015, turning material that might otherwise have gone to landfill into a component designed to sit beneath railway tracks. Developed by Integrated Recycling with researchers at Monash University's Institute of Railway Technology, the Duratrack sleeper is made from about 85% post-consumer plastic waste, including agricultural plastics, polystyrene and other difficult-to-recycle materials. After years of laboratory research and smaller railway trials, the sleepers reached Melbourne's metropolitan network in 2019, when about 190 were installed at Richmond station. Further testing followed at Tottenham Junction, where researchers monitored plastic and timber sleepers under real railway conditions. The sleepers were eventually approved for specified low-speed applications and have a potential lifespan of up to 50 years.Australia's plastic-to-railway experimentThe Duratrack project grew from an attempt to address two problems at the same time: the need for railway sleepers and the growing volume of plastic waste requiring new uses.Monash University's Institute of Railway Technology worked with Victorian manufacturer Integrated Recycling to develop a composite sleeper that could replace conventional materials such as timber. Research into the application of recycled plastic sleepers began in 2015, with government-backed research and development helping the technology move from development towards railway trials.The resulting Duratrack sleeper contains about 85% post-consumer plastic waste. The material includes agricultural plastics such as silage wrap and twine, as well as other waste streams including polystyrene. These materials were selected because they could otherwise have ended up in landfill or required other forms of disposal.Instead of treating the plastic as waste, the project turned it into a structural railway product.Researchers had to prove plastic could support railway tracksUsing recycled plastic in a railway sleeper required more than demonstrating that the material could be moulded into the right shape.Sleepers sit beneath rails and help transfer loads into the track structure. They must therefore withstand repeated forces while maintaining the geometry and stability of the railway.Monash researchers carried out laboratory testing of Duratrack to examine properties including its elastic modulus, maximum elastic strain limit and response to different strain rates. They also investigated load transfer, track stability, noise and vibration. Researchers developed a finite-element model using the measured properties to examine how factors such as track gauge and sleeper dimensions affected the material's behaviour.Before the sleepers reached Melbourne's metropolitan railway network, Duratrack had also been trialled on selected tourist and heritage railways in Victoria, including Puffing Billy, Walhalla Goldfields Railway and Victorian Goldfields Railway.These earlier trials provided experience with the material before it was subjected to testing on a metropolitan network.Nearly 200 plastic sleepers went under Melbourne trainsA major step came in June 2019, when Duratrack sleepers were installed at Richmond railway station in Melbourne.The first metropolitan trial involved about 190 sleepers as part of an 18-month trial. The Victorian government described the installation as the first use of the recycled-plastic sleepers on Melbourne's metropolitan train network.The sleepers were manufactured in Mildura by Integrated Recycling and contained recycled material sourced in Australia. The project was supported by Victorian government funding through Sustainability Victoria, with the research and development work led by Integrated Recycling and Monash University's Institute of Railway Technology.The Richmond installation was significant because it moved Duratrack beyond specialist heritage railways and into a working metropolitan railway environment.The government said the recycled sleepers had a potential lifespan of up to 50 years, while also describing them as requiring less maintenance than traditional timber sleepers.The 50-year figure is a potential service-life estimate, rather than evidence that the sleepers have already operated for five decades.The sleepers were tested alongside timberResearchers then carried out another in-track trial to examine how the recycled sleepers behaved under railway conditions.At Tottenham Junction in West Footscray, 25 Duratrack sleepers were installed in the Australian Rail Track Corporation network, interspersed with timber sleepers in a one-in-five arrangement. This allowed researchers to monitor the recycled sleepers within a track containing conventional timber sleepers.The research team monitored the sleepers over a 12-month period. Regular visual inspections were conducted, while researchers measured factors including strain, noise and vibration. The aim was to understand how the plastic composite behaved in actual track conditions and to improve the design procedures used for the sleepers.The results helped demonstrate that Duratrack could function as an alternative to timber sleepers for low-speed railway applications.That distinction matters because the product was not approved as a universal replacement for every type of railway sleeper. Its approval was focused on applications where its performance had been demonstrated.Plastic sleepers received approval for low-speed railThe research eventually helped create a pathway for Duratrack to move into real railway projects.The sleeper was type-approved for low-speed siding and yard applications on the Metro Trains Melbourne and V/Line networks. The research also contributed to the development of AS1085.22, an Australian Standard for alternative material sleepers, establishing a framework for railway sleepers made from materials other than conventional timber, concrete and steel.Duratrack sleepers subsequently appeared at locations including Richmond Station, Wyndham Vale stabling yard and Tottenham Station. The technology was also used in railway upgrade projects, with planned installations on the Shepparton and Warrnambool line upgrades.By this stage, the project had moved well beyond the question of whether plastic could technically be turned into a sleeper. The focus had shifted towards how the material could be incorporated into Australia's railway infrastructure.One kilometre of track can divert 64 tonnes of plasticThe environmental calculation provides another striking part of the project.Sustainability Victoria says that approximately 1,500 Duratrack sleepers, enough for about one kilometre of track, can divert around 64 tonnes of recyclable plastic from landfill.The sleepers are also designed with a circular-economy principle in mind. Sustainability Victoria says the composite sleepers can be recycled at the end of their service life and turned into new sleepers.The potential lifespan is another part of the argument for the material. Integrated Recycling has indicated that composite sleepers can last up to 50 years, while Victorian government material has described the lifespan as potentially three times that of traditional timber sleepers.The benefit, therefore, is not simply that plastic waste gets another use. The material is being converted into an infrastructure component intended to remain in service for decades.The technology moved towards larger-scale productionAs the railway trials progressed, Victoria also invested in increasing production capacity.In 2021, Integrated Recycling received funding through the Recycling Modernisation Fund to install a modular production line for Duratrack sleepers at its Mildura facility. The project was intended to allow the company to process an additional 1,600 tonnes of plastic and produce up to 35,000 sleepers a year.The expansion showed that the project was no longer being treated solely as a small research experiment. The aim was to create enough manufacturing capacity for recycled-plastic sleepers to become a practical option for railway infrastructure projects.The approach also offers a way of creating a domestic market for difficult-to-recycle plastics. Sustainability Victoria has identified recycled composite sleepers as a significant potential volume-use application for waste plastics in transport infrastructure.From discarded plastic to railway infrastructureWhat began as research in 2015 has therefore developed into a railway product that has undergone laboratory testing, heritage railway trials and testing on working metropolitan and mainline infrastructure.Duratrack is made from about 85% post-consumer recycled plastic, has been approved for specified low-speed railway applications and has been installed at multiple locations in Victoria.The potential lifespan of up to 50 years gives the technology an unusual long-term proposition, although that remains a projected lifespan rather than a result demonstrated through 50 years of operation.For every kilometre of track using roughly 1,500 of the sleepers, about 64 tonnes of recyclable plastic can be diverted from landfill.You use AI every day. articles.title: Stockton Globe generated no profit share for council last year
articles.summary: Stockton Council's deputy leader says the theatre is a "real asset" despite the lack of profit.
articles.body:
Councillors have been told a theatre is a "real asset" despite the local authority not receiving any profit from it last year.

Conservative group leader of Stockton Council, Tony Riordan, outlined the profit share agreement from 2019 which said the council would receive 30% of any of the Globe's earnings over £600,000 from year four of opening at a meeting on Wednesday.

It has been 10 years since the council took over the reins of the theatre's restoration, which was completed in 2021 after being empty since 1997.

The council's Labour deputy leader Paul Rowling acknowledged the council received no profit share for the 2025/26 financial year but said the Globe had put the town back on the map.

In 2021, the Grade II-listed theatre was said to have cost more than £30m once rental payments for the site were taken into account, with the council funding much of the project.

Council leaders hoped the Globe would bring an extra 200,000 visitors to the town every year and give the local economy an £18m boost.

Since opening, they said it had made "great progress" with 185,000 tickets sold worth more than £6m in its first two years, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.

But the Labour-led council has faced criticism from the Conservatives, who said it was a vanity project.

Rowling said the council received no profit share for the 2025/26 financial year, but saved the listed building from "further decline".

He also said the subsidy was included in the council's medium-term financial plan which was subject to approval each year, with "all groups" agreeing on it.

"The Globe's 3,000 capacity makes it the biggest live entertainment venue between Newcastle and Leeds, putting Stockton back on the map as a live entertainment destination," Rowling said.

The deputy leader added it was run by the Ambassador Theatre Group which operates venues worldwide, attracting "some of the world's best-known bands, artists and comedians".

"The people of Stockton deserve world-class facilities," he said.

"I think it's a real asset for the town centre and I think this fixation on pounds and pence isn't necessarily the way forward."

articles.title: Three in four households go hungry in parts of Yemen amid fighting: UN
articles.summary: World Food Programme warns of ‘devastating’ impact as conflict displaces thousands and cuts off food supplies.
articles.body:
Three out of four families in parts of Yemen are going hungry after a surge in fighting displaced tens of thousands of people and disrupted food supplies, the United Nations food agency says.

Some 74 percent of households in accessible government-held areas cannot meet their basic food needs, a record for this year, the World Food Programme (WFP) said on Friday.

An estimated 10 million people reside in government-held areas, according to WFP figures.

The rise in food insecurity indicates how quickly hunger is deepening in a country that imports about 90 percent of its food, as markets are disrupted and aid access shrinks.

In recent months, Yemen has faced a major escalation in fighting between Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-aligned Houthi group that controls parts of the country.

The latest flare-up “threatens to be absolutely devastating” for food security, said WFP’s Assistant Executive Director for Programme Operations Matthew Hollingworth.

“We are looking at a hunger crisis that is going to grow as it persists,” he added, speaking to reporters in Geneva via video link from Rome on Friday.

The Houthis, who already control most of northern Yemen including the capital Sanaa, seized the country’s Red Sea coast last month from the internationally recognised government, based in the southern port city of Aden.

Displaced families are arriving outside Aden and around Taiz with no food or water after leaving everything behind, the WFP said.

The WFP said it is scaling up its response to reach up to 1.5 million people, but it needs $109 million to do so.

It has already diverted resources from food distributions planned for November, and warns that without new funding, vulnerable displaced people will face gaps in assistance within a month.

Across Yemen, 18.3 million people face severe food insecurity, including 2.2 million acutely malnourished children under five, the WFP reported.

The fighting is widely described as the most serious escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis since a UN-brokered truce mostly halted cross-border attacks in 2022.

The conflict could reshape control of the country and further disrupt Red Sea shipping lanes.

Hollingworth warned that disruption around the Houthi-controlled Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Strait of Hormuz between Iran and the Gulf could push up food and fuel prices globally.

But the effects are already snowballing. More than 3,700 people fleeing the fighting had reached Djibouti via the Bab el-Mandeb Strait by late September, the WFP said.

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) says more than 149,000 people have been displaced in Yemen – many of them more than once.

articles.title: Nepal plans to drain four glacial lakes after deadly floods
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Nepal will kick off a high-stakes effort this fiscal year to drain four glacial lakes perched high in the mountains, as it scrambles to ⁠reduce flood risks, officials said, after a recent disaster that killed more than 1,400.
articles.body: KATHMANDU — Nepal will kick off a high-stakes effort this fiscal year to drain four glacial lakes perched high in the mountains, as it scrambles to ⁠reduce flood risks, officials said, after a recent disaster that killed more than 1,400. Rescuers are still searching for more than 5,000 people missing in the border region with China after August’s glacier collapse unleashed landslides and a flash flood that tore through valleys. “Our aim is to lower the risk of the lakes breaching their natural dams and reduce the risk of downstream floods,” said Subash Tuladhar, an expert with a government research centre tasked ⁠with overseeing the new project. Canals will drain water into nearby ​rivers ⁠in a regulated way, he said, adding that workers faced health risks as a result of the lengthy periods of high-altitude work required, in addition to the dangers of sudden flooding. Design work and detailed studies targeting the ⁠central and eastern lakes of Thulagi, Lower Barun, Lumding Tsho and Hongu II, will begin in the fiscal year that ​runs until ⁠mid-July 2027, authorities said. The lakes, at heights ranging from ‌4,050 m to 5,483 m (13,280 ft to 18,000 ft), rank among Nepal’s most potentially dangerous, the United Nations Development Programme and the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) said in a 2020 report. Nepal had the skills and experience required for ‌the $50-million project to be funded by the Green Climate Fund, the UNDP and ‌the government, added Tuladhar, of Nepal’s Centre for Hydrology and Water Resources Research. Draining project could take six years The work of draining “through gated structures” will start after a detailed study, and could take up to six years to complete, said Sanjeeb Baral, the Centre’s executive director. It will encompass installation of sensors, a ⁠flood forecasting and warning system, and efforts to build downstream resilience and prepare communities for the risks. In similar previous efforts, Nepal lowered by 3 m (10 ft) the level of the central Himalayan glacial lake of Tsho Rolpa in 2000, and that of Imja in the vicinity of Mount Everest, the world’s tallest peak, 10 years ago. Urgency after recent floods Nepal’s disaster served as a warning to the world, Prime Minister Balendra Shah, 36, told the United Nations in an impassioned speech last month that blamed climate change despite his country’s negligible emissions. Retreating glaciers, unstable mountain slopes and increasingly unpredictable rivers showed Nepal was paying a heavy price, he ‌added. Nepal, which has reported about 26 Glacial Lake Outburst Flood events in the past four decades, loses ​more than 300 lives and property worth millions of dollars to extreme climate events annually on average. The latest floods ‌devastated a dozen hydroelectric plants, roads, bridges, farms and settlements. ⁠Cash-strapped Nepal would need nearly $5 billion for early recovery, officials have said. Climate scientists say as temperatures rise ⁠glaciers in the Himalayas retreat, leaving behind unstable glacial lakes held back by little more than loose rock and ice, above valleys home to millions. Lowering the lakes by ‌3 m (10 ft) would significantly reduce the ​threat, said Samjwal Ratna Bajracharya, a retired ICIMOD expert on glaciers, ‌glacial lakes and outburst floods. “They are growing fast, ​are high up in the Himalayas and could cause outbursts any time, due to earthquakes, avalanches, climatic conditions and unplanned human-induced activity,” he told Reuters.

articles.body: A sexual assault lawsuit involving a Cornell University fraternity has thrust an often-overlooked part of New York's rape law into the spotlight, prompting renewed calls to change how the state handles cases involving intoxicated victims. The issue gained new attention after Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten initially declined to file criminal charges stemming from allegations that a woman was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house in 2024. Gov. Kathy Hochul has since appointed Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor to oversee the criminal investigation while also calling for lawmakers to revisit the state's consent laws. MAMDANI ROASTED OVER ASSERTION THAT HIGHER NYC RAPES COME FROM 'EXPANDED DEFINITION' The Associated Press reported the renewed focus centers on what critics have dubbed the "voluntary intoxication loophole," a provision in New York law that can make it more difficult to prosecute certain sexual assault cases involving voluntarily intoxicated victims. New York criminal defense attorney and former Manhattan prosecutor Mark Bederow said the debate largely turns on one legal concept: mental incapacity. Under New York law, a person who is mentally incapacitated cannot legally consent to sexual activity. But Bederow said the statute draws an important distinction between someone who unknowingly became intoxicated and someone who voluntarily consumed alcohol or drugs. "If somebody slipped you something like a date rape drug and it somehow severely impacted your mental capacity, but you didn't voluntarily take that, that very well would support a theory of lack of consent," Bederow told Fox News Digital. "But if you drink yourself into an oblivion, that theory of lack of consent as a matter of law would not apply." CONVICTED PREDATORS FACE LIFETIME BARRIER UNDER GOP LAWMAKER’S SWEEPING VICTIM PROTECTION BILL "If you change this law, you're going to have situations where people are later asked to determine whether someone truly lacked the capacity to consent or whether they consented in the moment and later regretted it," he said. Although the proposal has received support from prosecutors and victim advocates, it has repeatedly stalled. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST Hochul has now thrown her support behind changing the law. articles.title: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel after Trump export ban threat
articles.summary: The coordinated release is aimed at heading off further price spikes and avoiding a ban on US diesel exports.
articles.body:
The G7 has agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel in a bid to ease supply pressures that have caused prices to skyrocket.

The group of advanced economies, including the US, said the move would include a "substantial release" of diesel in the coming days.

President Donald Trump had threatened to ban diesel exports in a move which would have eased pressure on prices for US consumers ahead of November's midterm elections, but pushed up prices elsewhere.

In a joint statement, the G7 said member countries had now agreed to "refrain from export restrictions on energy and energy products" on one another.

The G7 includes the US, UK, Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France, with the EU also represented at its meetings.

Trump had warned he would ban diesel exports from the US if European countries did not agree to put more of their own stocks onto the market.

On Friday, he said on social media: "Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately."

His Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had argued US farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar.

Diesel is used heavily by the haulage industry and in agriculture, meaning rises in the cost of the fuel feed through into essentials such as food.

But, following a meeting of G7 leaders, French President Emmanuel Macron said the bloc had agreed to release reserves of "up to 100 million barrels" within four months under the coordination of the International Energy Agency (IEA).

The UK was represented at the meeting by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who said the measures would "stabilise energy supplies, build resilience in supply chains and shield households and businesses from price shocks".

Macron said the coordinated action would "bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel". Highlighting the agreement not to pursue export bans, Macron said "President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point".

In the joint statement, G7 leaders said: "We will implement our commitments with a coordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels to begin immediately over four months, including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners."

It is not yet clear which partner countries will release stocks, nor how quickly.

The 100 million barrels will comprise a mix of diesel and crude oil. The price of global benchmark Brent crude oil briefly dropped below $100 a barrel, but rose back to around $102 by Friday evening. Before the US and Israel invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73.

European countries had pushed back against US threats to turn off American diesel, against a backdrop of the US-led war in the Middle East and reduced supplies from Russia and China.

The G7 leaders said they will also coordinate maintenance schedules to avoid multiple refineries being shut down at the same time, while encouraging countries with the capacity to do so to ramp up refining of diesel in particular.

Why UK diesel prices have breached the £2 per litre mark

Avoiding a ban on US diesel exports will offer significant relief to countries which are reliant on imports of the fuel, including the UK, where prices at the pump topped £2 a litre for the first time on Friday .

Over half of the UK's diesel is imported, with 31% of those imports coming from the US.

The US is one of the world's leading diesel suppliers, with domestic refineries churning out roughly four to five million barrels every day, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA).

Americans consume about 3.6 million barrels of that. Refiners export the remaining 1.2 to 1.5 million barrels per day, making the US a vital supplier to the global market.

Supplies of diesel internationally have been heavily constrained by the conflict in the Middle East, which has restricted the flow of both crude oil and refined diesel onto global markets.

Russia, which is also a major producer, has implemented its own export ban on diesel, following attacks on its refineries by Ukraine, further limiting supply. The G7 leaders stressed that they will maintain sanctions against Russia amid its ongoing war in Ukraine.

Diesel is harder to refine than petrol and, because of its use in the haulage industry and agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand.

articles.title: SIR under review:  Former SC, HC judges to examine 'constitutional & statutory validity' of voter roll revision
articles.summary: A panel of five former Supreme Court and high court judges has been set up by a lawyers' body to examine the Election Commission’s Special Intensive
articles.body: A panel of five former Supreme Court and high court judges has been set up by a lawyers' body to examine the Election Commission’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, as the poll panel separately moves to identify and re-enrol voters left out during the exercise.The Lawyers Association for Constitution (LAFC) said the commission, headed by former Supreme Court judge Madan B Lokur, will examine the constitutional and statutory validity of the SIR, its methodology and its overall impact on eligible voters, reported PTI."The newly-formed independent commission of former judges on the Special Intensive Revision of the electoral roll will function with complete autonomy to examine the constitutional and statutory validity, methodology and overall impact of the SIR exercise on eligible voters," it said.The other members are former Supreme Court judge A K Patnaik, former chief justice of the Jammu and Kashmir High Court Badar Durrez Ahmad, and former judges Rekha Sharma and Anjana Prakash.Meanwhile, LAFC said senior lawyers including Kapil Sibal, Prashant Bhushan, Chander Uday Singh, Prashanto Chandra Sen, Raju Ramachandran, Rebecca Mammen John, Warisha Farasat and Vrinda Grover will provide strategic legal advice to the commission.The commission will examine whether eligible citizens were retained on the electoral roll and whether ineligible entries were appropriately excluded, the LAFC said.It plans to hold public hearings across the country, with full and regional benches travelling to different locations to record the views and testimonies of affected citizens, civil society organisations and experts.The LAFC said the commission would function with complete autonomy and have the final responsibility for its findings and recommendations.The panel's formation comes as the Election Commission has directed state poll officials to launch a special drive to identify and enrol valid voters who were left out after the SIR in states where the exercise has been completed.Under the drive, Booth Level Officers will compare current electoral rolls with pre-SIR lists to identify electors whose names were earlier included but later dropped. They will then conduct house-to-house verification of the identified voters.The BLOs have also been asked to collect Form 6 applications on the spot from eligible first-time voters and genuine left-out electors. The exercise is targeted for completion within a month, with each BLO expected to cover 20 to 25 electors a week.The move follows the Election Commission's September 26 decision to withdraw an additional SIR-related declaration attached to Form 6 in states where the revision has been completed. New applicants in these states will now submit the regular statutory Form 6.The additional declaration remains available in states and Union territories where SIR is still under way.
